title: Monitoring
subtitle: Is it holding up against real visitors?
intro_md:
The monitor compares what the live model predicts against what it predicted back on its training data. Every tracked signal has drifted — real visitors doodle differently than the dataset, and mean confidence has slid from {confidenceFrom} to {confidenceTo}.

That's not the model failing; that's the instrument catching the world moving — and it's exactly what the retrain flywheel feeds on.

sections.title: Output drift
sections.body: Drift is measured on what the model *outputs*, not on the pixels going in — the log deliberately never keeps anyone's drawing. Three signals are tracked, each scored against the training-era baseline.

signals.label: Which classes it guesses
signals.plain: The mix of answers the model gives. Shifts when visitors draw different things than the dataset did.

signals.label: Top-1 confidence
signals.plain: How sure the model is of its best guess. A slide here is the earliest sign real drawings are harder than training ones.

signals.label: Top-1 vs top-2 margin
signals.plain: How far the winning guess beats the runner-up. A thinner margin means more genuine toss-ups.

sections.note: The report measures drift but doesn't cry wolf about it: out-of-distribution drift is constant and expected, so it only raises an alert when the model is actually doing badly — a confidence collapse or a failing accuracy signal.

sections.title: Proxy accuracy from feedback
sections.body: Every time a visitor grades a guess with yes or no, that verdict becomes a running stand-in for real-world accuracy — overall, per class, and by input type.

emptyState.label: n = 0
emptyState.text: A quiet week with no verdicts is a valid result, not an error — the drift signals carry the page until the next visitor grades a guess.

footer: Drift is computed weekly by Evidently over the model's own outputs; feedback is the retrain flywheel's label source.
